assumptions: Impact duration is not established. The incident record shows 48 seconds, but that is the automation's investigation window; the flag was still on and the error rate still 33% at the last log line. Any cost estimate must use the interval from 22:07 to the time a human disabled the flag, taken from the flag audit log, not the incident record.

The 27.5% headline error rate is taken as given and is consistent with the per-minute WARN lines (25%, 34%, 32%, 32%, 28%, 33%). It is the account-page error rate; it is assumed here to be the share of account-page traffic that failed, not the share of all io-shop traffic.

The ERROR lines are clearly sampled — two per minute cannot produce a 33% rate against 200 evaluations per minute — so failure counts were inferred from the WARN percentages rather than counted from log lines.

Traffic is assumed flat at roughly 200 account-page evaluations per minute throughout, because that is the only volume figure in the logs and it does not vary across the window. 22:07-22:13 is late evening UTC and real traffic may be lower or higher than a daily average.

The ~1-2% baseline of UpstreamTimeout errors on payment authorization predates the incident and continues through it. Those failures are treated as background and excluded from incident impact; they are a separate, pre-existing issue worth its own ticket.
No deploy was recorded in the 24-hour change window, and the log sample provided contains no deploy events. The conclusion that no release was involved rests on that change record being complete.

The specific data condition that makes the denominator zero for some accounts was not identified from the logs; that a subset of accounts triggers it is inferred from the error rate sitting near a third rather than at 100%.
No remediation was performed by the automation: zero actions were taken and none were undone, so the system was left in the state that caused the incident.
input.executive_summary:
Starting at 22:07 UTC on 2 September 2026, roughly a third of visits to the account page on the shop service failed with an error and showed the customer a broken page. The cause was a newly switched-on feature that displays a customer's monthly spend; for some accounts the calculation behind it was invalid and crashed the page. Customers browsing or buying elsewhere on the site were unaffected, as were the parts of the account page that did not depend on the new feature — but any customer who hit the failure could not view their account details until they retried and happened to land on a working request.

Automated response opened an incident at 22:12 and correctly identified the cause within seconds, reaching the same conclusion on three independent passes with high confidence. However, it was not permitted to act: turning the feature back off was not among the reversible actions available to it, so every proposed remedy was blocked at the safety gate. No change was made to the system, and the incident was handed to a human at 22:13 with the failure still ongoing. The 0.01-hour figure on the incident record measures how long the automation spent on the case, not how long customers were affected; customer impact began at 22:07 and the logs give no evidence of it ending. Anyone reading this should assume impact continued until a person turned the flag off, and should confirm that time from the flag audit log.

The immediate fix is to disable the `monthly-spend-feature` flag. The follow-ups are to guard the spend calculation against a zero denominator before re-enabling, and to add "roll back a feature flag" to the set of actions the automated responder is allowed to take on its own, since this incident was diagnosed correctly and quickly but could not be stopped.
input.impact_weight_reason: The failing path is the account page, not a checkout or cart. Nothing in the evidence shows a purchase completing through this page, and the errors are confined to it — there is no sign of elevated failures on browse or checkout traffic. Most affected visitors were doing account admin and would simply return later, so the great majority of these failed requests carried no revenue. It is not zero, though, for two reasons visible in the logs: the account page calls payment authorization (the baseline UpstreamTimeout errors come from that call), so it sits close enough to billing that some sessions there are payment-method or subscription management that can lapse if abandoned; and the broken feature is a spend display, which is the kind of thing an unhappy customer looks at right before cancelling. 0.15 reflects a page where a small minority of visits have money attached and nearly everyone else comes back.
input.root_cause: The `monthly-spend-feature` flag on io-shop was flipped from off to on at 22:07 (roughly 78% of evaluations on in that first minute, 100% on from 22:08), and the code path it enables computes a monthly spend figure by dividing by a value that is zero for a subset of accounts, raising ZeroDivisionError on the account page. No deploy was recorded in the preceding 24 hours (or week), so the toggle — not a release — is what exposed the latent defect; the account-page error rate stepped from a ~0-2% baseline of unrelated payment-authorization timeouts to 25-34% in the same minute the flag moved.
